Before he ever defended a client, Jason stood in court as a prosecutor. In 1996, he tried his first DUI case from the State’s side of the courtroom. That early experience shaped how he understands criminal law today.

Prosecutors are trained to build cases. They evaluate evidence, prepare witnesses, and construct arguments designed to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. Jason learned how that process works from the inside—how decisions are made, how weaknesses are evaluated, and how cases are presented.
Years later, as a criminal defense attorney, he uses that same knowledge in reverse.
Instead of building cases, he takes them apart.

This dual perspective is not theoretical. It influences every decision made in a case—from the first review of police reports to the final resolution. It allows him to anticipate how the prosecution will approach the case and to identify issues before they fully develop.
People sometimes assume that criminal cases are straightforward. They believe that if an arrest was made, the evidence must be solid. In reality, criminal cases are rarely that simple.

Every case is built on layers of interpretation and procedure. Officers observe behavior and draw conclusions. Evidence is collected and documented. Witnesses provide statements that may or may not be consistent over time.
Jason approaches every case with a fundamental understanding that there is no such thing as a perfect investigation. Police officers are human. Systems are imperfect. Details are overlooked.
The goal of a criminal defense attorney is not to accept the case as presented. It is to examine it critically.
That process often involves looking closely at:
Whether the initial stop or detention was lawful Whether probable cause truly existed at the time of arrest Whether procedures were followed correctly Whether the evidence tells a consistent story
In many cases, it is not one major flaw that changes the outcome. It is a combination of smaller issues, each one raising questions, that together create reasonable doubt.

Maximizing Protection Under the Bankruptcy Code

One of the most important aspects of any bankruptcy case is the proper use of legal protections. The Bankruptcy Code provides powerful tools, but those tools must be applied correctly to be fully effective.
Erin’s practice is focused on ensuring that clients receive the full benefit of those protections.

This includes evaluating which chapter of bankruptcy is most appropriate, whether Chapter 7 or Chapter 13, based on the client’s income, assets, and long-term goals. It also includes careful attention to exemption laws, which determine what property can be protected during the bankruptcy process.

Washington State provides specific exemptions designed to allow individuals to retain essential assets. These may include a primary residence, a vehicle, retirement accounts, and personal property. Erin’s experience allows her to structure cases in a way that aligns with these protections, ensuring that clients are positioned as strongly as possible under the law.
Understanding Bankruptcy as a Structured Solution
There is often a great deal of confusion surrounding bankruptcy. Many people approach it with uncertainty, influenced by misconceptions or incomplete information.

In reality, bankruptcy is a carefully designed legal system. It exists to address situations where debt has become unmanageable and where repayment is no longer realistic. The purpose of the law is not to punish individuals, but to provide a structured path toward financial recovery.
Erin’s role is to help clients understand that system.

She works to explain not just what bankruptcy is, but how it works in practical terms. What debts can be discharged. What obligations may remain. What protections are available immediately upon filing, such as the automatic stay, which stops collection activity, lawsuits, and wage garnishments.
This clarity is essential. It allows clients to move forward with confidence, knowing exactly what to expect at each stage of the process.
For many individuals, Chapter 7 bankruptcy offers the most direct path to meaningful financial relief.

When a person qualifies for Chapter 7, most unsecured debts can be discharged. This typically includes credit cards, medical bills, personal loans, and other forms of unsecured financial obligations. Once the discharge is entered, those debts are permanently eliminated.
This process occurs within a relatively short timeframe. In many cases, a discharge is granted within a few months of filing.

Erin works closely with clients to determine whether Chapter 7 is appropriate and to ensure that the process is handled in a way that maximizes the available protections. This includes careful preparation of all required documentation and a thorough understanding of how the case will be evaluated.

You hire us, and we handle everything.

For decades, Jason S. Newcombe and the attorneys who work with him have helped clients throughout Western Washington resolve traffic violations efficiently and effectively. Over the years, they have handled—and favorably resolved—thousands of traffic tickets. Jason S. Newcombe has been handling traffic infractions and criminal driving cases for more than 30 years. Over that time, he has developed a detailed understanding of how these cases are built and how they can be challenged. What may appear to be a straightforward citation is often based on multiple layers of evidence that must meet specific legal standards.

Traffic tickets are typically built on officer observations, technical measurements such as radar or lidar, and written reports that must be accurate and complete. If any part of that process falls short, it can create an opportunity to challenge the validity of the ticket. Jason’s approach is not to assume that a ticket is correct simply because it was issued. Instead, each case is carefully analyzed to determine whether the evidence actually supports the citation. That process often reveals weaknesses that can be used to pursue a dismissal or reduction.

Challenging Speeding Tickets and Other Violations

Speeding tickets are among the most common citations issued in Washington State, but they are not always as straightforward as they appear. Many of these cases rely on radar or lidar readings that must be properly calibrated, correctly operated, and accurately documented.

If there is a flaw in how the reading was obtained or recorded, the ticket may be challenged. These types of issues arise more often than people expect, and they can make a meaningful difference in the outcome of a case.

Our firm regularly handles standard speeding tickets, as well as violations involving school zones and construction zones. Each case is carefully reviewed to determine whether the evidence supports the citation or whether it can be successfully challenged.
HOV Violations and Observation-Based Tickets

HOV and carpool lane violations have become increasingly common throughout Western Washington. These tickets are often based on quick observations made by law enforcement in real-time traffic conditions.

Those observations are not always accurate or complete. By carefully reviewing the circumstances surrounding the stop, it is often possible to identify inconsistencies or gaps in the evidence that can be used to challenge the ticket.

Some traffic violations carry more serious consequences and require a more strategic defense. Negligent Driving in the First Degree, for example, is a criminal offense that can impact your record, your insurance, and your future.

Jason’s background in criminal law allows him to approach these cases with the level of detail they require. Even Negligent Driving in the Second Degree, which is more common, often relies on subjective interpretations of driving behavior. Those interpretations can be challenged when they are not supported by clear and objective evidence.
